report:
**Conclusion: no—the best current evidence does not show that ginkgo extract reliably relieves tinnitus.**

The most rigorous recent assessment, a 2022 Cochrane review, found **no evidence of benefit versus placebo** for tinnitus severity or loudness. It included randomized trials but judged several outcome estimates as low/very-low certainty, meaning a small benefit cannot be ruled out completely; however, the results do not support recommending it.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD013514_ginkgo-biloba-herbal-supplement-tinnitus

Why might your sister have heard “yes”? Older trials and reviews have produced mixed findings, often involving different ginkgo preparations, doses, populations, and outcome measures. But when tinnitus is the main problem—as opposed to being a symptom in studies of dementia or vascular disease—the more reliable synthesis has not found a meaningful, reproducible effect.

Clinical guidance aligns with this: the American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery guideline recommends **against** ginkgo (as well as melatonin and zinc) for persistent, bothersome tinnitus.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25273878/

**Safety:** “Natural” does not mean risk-free. Cochrane reported no serious adverse events in the included tinnitus trials, but certainty for bleeding/seizure outcomes was low. Ginkgo can interact with medicines, particularly anticoagulant/antiplatelet drugs; discuss it with a clinician or pharmacist before taking it, especially before procedures or if using regular medications.  
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ginkgo

More evidence-supported care is assessment for hearing loss and individualized tinnitus management (for example, hearing support when indicated and psychological interventions for tinnitus-related distress). Seek prompt medical evaluation for sudden hearing loss with tinnitus, heartbeat-synchronous noise, or new neurologic symptoms.  
https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/tinnitus/
